title.en: Ramayana — Balakanda (Wikipedia summary story — Telugu, full text)

lessons.title: Lesson 01 — Introduction
lessons.content: The story of Balakanda is briefly narrated here.

lessons.title: Lesson 02 — Beginning of the Epic
lessons.content:
Once, Sage Narada visited Sage Valmiki’s hermitage. When Valmiki asked if there was a man possessed of all excellences, Narada narrated the story of Rama. Rama was devoted to truth and duty, a great hero, possessed of unmatched virtues, and delight of all. The story of Rama is supremely sacred and the essence of all Vedas.

Later, when Valmiki went to bathe in the Tamasa river, he saw a hunter kill a bird and spontaneously composed the shloka: 'Ma Nishada...'. Afterwards, Brahma appeared and commanded Valmiki to compose the Ramayana in such verses. He blessed that the story of Sita and Rama would remain immortal as long as mountains and rivers endure.

In his meditation, Valmiki realized the entire Ramayana with all secrets, then composed it sweetly with every aspect of virtue and desire. The Ramayana consists of 24,000 verses in total and 500 chapters (including Uttara Kanda). Kusha and Lava learned from Valmiki and joyously sang the Rama story for all.

lessons.title: Lesson 03 — Ayodhya City, Birth of Rama
lessons.content:
Dasharatha of the glorious Ikshvaku lineage was a Vedic scholar, valiant, and righteous. He ruled the prosperous kingdom of Kosala from the joyous capital Ayodhya. Childless, he became distressed and resolved, with his ministers and priests’ blessings, to perform a sacrificial rite. He invited Shanta, daughter of his cousin king Romapada, and her husband Rishyashringa to Ayodhya. Rishyashringa officiated the Ashwamedha sacrifice and then performed the Putrakameshti.

By the satisfaction of the gods from these rites, Vishnu resolved to take human birth as four sons to Dasharatha to destroy Ravana. Ravana, protected from death by gods, demons, gandharvas, yakshas, and rakshasas, was tormenting the gods; only humans and monkeys could kill him.

Dasharatha gave the sacrificial pudding to his wives Kausalya, Kaikeyi, and Sumitra, who conceived sons. On Chaitra Navami, under Punarvasu star, Kausalya bore Rama; Kaikeyi bore Bharata under Pushyami and Meena lagna; Sumitra bore Lakshmana and Shatrughna under Ashlesha and Karkataka lagna. Sage Vashistha named the sons. The four brothers excelled in virtues, education, and won everyone’s hearts. Among them, Rama specially shone as the dearest to Dasharatha and all people, and Lakshmana never left Rama’s side.

The gods created vanara and bear warriors with their energies. With Brahma’s part: Jambavan; Indra’s: Vali; Surya’s: Sugriva; Brihaspati’s: Tara; Vishwakarma’s: Nala; Agni’s: Nila; Kubera’s: Gandhamadana; Ashvini’s: Mainda and Dvivida; Varuna’s: Sushena; Parjanya’s: Sharabha — these valiant vanara and bear troops grew to aid Rama in Ravana’s destruction. With Vayu’s part: Hanuman, unmatched in valor, energy, and quickness, and body as hard as diamond, was born.

lessons.title: Lesson 04 — Discipleship under Vishwamitra
lessons.content:
Once Sage Vishwamitra came to Ayodhya, requesting Dasharatha to send Rama, who was fifteen years old, to protect his sacrifice from the demons Maricha and Subahu, who were constantly destroying it. Dasharatha pleaded to go himself with an army, doubting a boy could fight such demons, but Vishwamitra insisted. After being encouraged by Sage Vashistha, Dasharatha sent Rama and Lakshmana with Vishwamitra.

On the way, Vishwamitra first taught Rama the lustrous mantras Bala and Atibala, which protect from fatigue and hunger. They spent one night resting, and in the morning, Vishwamitra awakened Rama saying: 'May Kausalya’s womb be blessed, Rama, wake up, perform morning rituals.'

lessons.title: Lesson 05 — The Slaying of Tataka, Protection of the Sacrifice
lessons.content:
On another night, after resting at Manmadha’s hermitage, they entered the terrifying Tataka forest. The formidable and magical demoness Tataka attacked them. At his guru’s command, Rama slew Tataka with his arrow.

The next day, Vishwamitra blessed Rama and Lakshmana, granting them many divine weapons and their use and withdrawal mantras. They entered Vishwamitra’s Siddhashram, the former ashram of Trivikrama (Vamana incarnation). Vishwamitra assigned Rama and Lakshmana to guard the ashram and the sacrifice, then commenced the ritual. Maricha, Subahu, and their demon band gathered in the sky to disrupt the sacrifice. Rama hurled Maricha with a Shakti weapon into the ocean, killed Subahu with an Agneyastra, and routed the rest with a Vayavyastra. The sacrifice ended peacefully. Joyful Vishwamitra blessed them.

The next day, Vishwamitra took Rama and Lakshmana with him to witness King Janaka’s sacrifice at Mithila City.

lessons.title: Lesson 06 — The Lineage of Vishwamitra
lessons.content:
On the banks of the Shona river, Vishwamitra narrated his lineage to Rama and Lakshmana:
Kusha was a pious sage, married to the princess of Vidarbha. Of their four sons, Kushanabha married apsara Ghritachi and had a hundred daughters. Once, after refusing Vayu’s proposal, the daughters were cursed and became hunchbacked.

The princess Somada, daughter of Urmila, by the favor of Sage Chuli became mother of Brahmadatta. Brahmadatta, now a king, agreed to marry all hundred hunchbacked daughters of Kushanabha. At his touch, they returned to their celestial beauty.

Later, Kushanabha performed sacrifices and obtained his son Gadhi. Gadhi and Somada’s son was Vishwamitra. Vishwamitra’s sister Satyavati married sage Richika and afterwards became the river Kausiki. Vishwamitra resided on its bank.

lessons.title: Lesson 07 — The Descent of the Ganga
lessons.content:
At Rama’s request, Vishwamitra narrated the birth of Kumaraswami (Kartikeya) and the descent of Mother Ganga:

Shiva’s fiery seed was received by Agni and Ganga. Unable to bear it, Ganga deposited it at the foothills of the Himalayas, whence shweta mountain and grass appeared. Kartikeya, nourished by six Krittikas, was crowned commander-in-chief by all the gods.

King Sagara of Ayodhya had Asamanjas by his first wife Keshini and sixty thousand sons by his second wife Sumati. Asamanjas’ son Anshuman was beloved of all. During Sagara’s Ashwamedha sacrifice, Indra stole the ritual horse. Sagara's sixty thousand sons, searching for the horse, dug deep into the earth, reached the netherworld, worshipped the giants, continued digging, and arrived at Kapila’s hermitage. Mistaking Kapila, who was near the horse, the sons accused him, and by his wrath, they were all burnt to ashes.

Anshuman reached the netherworld, mourned over his uncles’ ashes, and Garuda advised doing tarpana (mourning rites) for their souls with the waters of Ganga. Anshuman retrieved the horse, allowing Sagara to complete the sacrifice. Anshuman ruled after Sagara, followed by his son Dilipa, who performed twelve thousand years of austerities. Dilipa’s son Bhagiratha did a thousand years of penance for Ganga’s descent. Brahma granted the wish, but said only Shiva could bear Ganga’s fall; Bhagiratha’s penance to Shiva succeeded, and Shiva held Ganga in his hair.

With a single stream, Ganga descended, purifying along her course. Angered by Ganga flooding his hermitage, Sage Jahnu drank her in, but at the gods’ request, released her from his ear; hence she is called Jahnavi. Ganga reached the ocean, entered the netherworld, and, flowing over the ashes of Sagara’s sons, blessed them with salvation.

After resting in the city of Vishala, Vishwamitra narrated to Rama and Lakshmana the story of the churning of the milk ocean and the tale of Marutta. King Sumati of Vishala welcomed them.

lessons.title: Lesson 08 — The Story of Ahalya
lessons.content:
On the way to Mithila, they saw the deserted hermitage of Sage Gautama. Once, Indra, disguised as Gautama, united with Ahalya, Gautama’s wife. Discovering the deception, Gautama cursed Indra and Ahalya; Indra was transformed into a ram and covered with a thousand eyes, while Ahalya became invisible and survived only on air, like a moon hidden by a cloud or fire by smoke.

When Rama entered the ashram, Ahalya’s curse was lifted, she became visible, and Rama and Lakshmana touched her feet. With devotion, she worshipped them, and Gautama returned and together honored their guests.

Satisfied, Vishwamitra, Rama, and Lakshmana proceeded to Mithila, where King Janaka invited them to his sacrificial hall. Vishwamitra introduced Rama and Lakshmana.

lessons.title: Lesson 09 — The Story of Vishwamitra
lessons.content:
Janaka's priest Shatananda, son of Ahalya and Gautama, rejoiced at hearing of his mother’s deliverance. He narrated Vishwamitra’s history of penance:

Vishwamitra, son of Gadhi, was once a great king. He once visited Sage Vashistha’s hermitage, where Vashistha, with the divine cow Shabala, splendidly entertained him and his entire army. Vishwamitra tried to buy Shabala with gold and cattle, but Vashistha refused; Vishwamitra tried to seize Shabala by force.

Shabala, with Vashistha’s permission, created a mighty army that defeated Vishwamitra’s force. Vishwamitra’s weapons failed. He performed austerities to Shiva, obtained all divine weapons, and again attacked Vashistha’s hermitage, but his Brahmadanda was invincible. Even Brahmastra failed.

Recognizing the futility of force, Vishwamitra undertook severe austerities. Brahma gave him the title Rajarshi, but Vishwamitra was still not satisfied. Later, to fulfill king Trishanku’s wish, Vishwamitra created another heaven; as long as the worlds exist, his creation remains apart from the Vishwanara path.

At Pushkara, he saved Sunasshepa, who was to be sacrificed in Ambarisha’s ritual. After another thousand years of penance, Brahma named him Maharshi, but he sought further perfection. Despite disturbances from Menaka, Indra, and Rambha, he continued his penance. Eventually, Brahma and Vashistha acclaimed him as Brahmarshi.

lessons.title: Lesson 10 — The Decision of Marriage
lessons.content:
Once, while ploughing the field for a sacrifice, King Janaka found a daughter in the furrow. He named her Sita ('furrow-born'), raising her himself. He declared that whoever could string the bow of Shiva would wed her. The divine bow had always been worshipped at Janaka’s palace and none had ever strung it before.

At Vishwamitra’s request, Janaka displayed Shiva’s bow to the Raghu princes. With approval, Rama easily lifted and strung the bow, which broke with a resounding noise. Delighted, Janaka determined, by his vow, Rama was worthy to wed Sita; with Vishwamitra’s agreement, he sent word to King Dasharatha. Dasharatha, with his family, arrived at Mithila, was honored by Janaka, and expressed readiness to accept Sita as daughter-in-law. Janaka’s sacrifice ended joyfully.

Janaka’s brother Kushadhvaja also arrived for the great assembly. On Vishwamitra’s request, Vashistha described the Ikshvaku lineage, and Janaka narrated his own. The sages consulted and agreed: Rama would marry Sita, Lakshmana to Urmila, Bharata to Mandavi, and Shatrughna to Shrutakirti. Janaka, delighted, requested all four weddings to be held under the auspicious Uttara Phalguni star.

lessons.title: Lesson 11 — The Marriage of Sita and Rama
lessons.content: After completing auspicious rites like donating cows, Dasharatha arrived with his sons, awaiting the bridegivers. In the splendid wedding mandap, Janaka installed the sacred fire and performed rituals with Vashistha, Vishwamitra, and Shatananda present. Sita, adorned in jewels, was brought, and Janaka said: 'O Rama, son of Kausalya, here is my daughter Sita, your co-partner in dharma. Accept her hand; she will always follow you like a shadow.’ He poured consecrated water into Rama’s hands. Divine drums sounded in the heavens; flowers showered down. With Vashistha’s blessing, Rama married Sita, Lakshmana married Urmila, Bharata married Mandavi, and Shatrughna married Shrutakirti. They all circled the sacred fire, Janaka, and the sages. The marriages of Sita-Rama and their brothers were celebrated grandly for the welfare of the world. They returned to their quarters with the sage-friends.

lessons.title: Lesson 12 — Humbling of Parashurama’s Pride
lessons.content:
After receiving everyone’s honors, Vishwamitra departed to the Himalayas. Dasharatha took leave of Janaka, and with the newlyweds, set out for Ayodhya. Then a fierce storm arose, and Parashurama, radiant as fire and like Mount Kailasa, appeared. Vashistha and other sages worshipped him.

Parashurama challenged: 'Dasharatha Rama, I heard you broke Shiva’s bow. Here is my Jamadagni bow: string it, draw an arrow, and show your strength; then I will duel you.’ He ignored all Dasharatha’s pleas, demanded Rama to string his divine bow, and incensed, Rama did so. Since a divine arrow should not be wasted, he would destroy either Parashurama’s life regions or those gained by penance. Parashurama, humbled, requested Rama not to destroy his paralyzed feet but to take away his attained heavenly regions. Realizing Rama was the eternal incarnation of Vishnu, Parashurama was not ashamed; Rama shot the arrow, and Parashurama departed for Mahendra Mountain to resume his penance.

lessons.title: Lesson 13 — Return to Ayodhya
lessons.content:
Joyful at their renewal, Dasharatha returned with his ministers, sons, and daughters-in-law to Ayodhya. The daughters-in-law greeted their mothers-in-law, received blessings, worshipped in temples, and entered their homes. The brothers received elders’ blessings and settled with their wives.

After some days, Bharata and Shatrughna went to their uncle’s house. Sita and Rama served elders and each other happily. Blessed with the incomparable princess Sita, Rama shone like Vishnu united with Lakshmi.
